Plaintiff, appearing pro se, opposes Defendant's motion to dismiss (ECF No. [[NUMBER]]).

## I. Introduction

1. Defendant asks the Court to hold that a Member of Congress may open an official account to public comment, invite constituents to respond, and then exclude one constituent because of the view she expressed. The First Amendment does not permit that, and none of Defendant's grounds reaches it.

## II. The Account Is Government Action

2. Defendant says the Account is personal. The test is not what Defendant calls it. The test is whether she "possessed actual authority to speak on the State's behalf" and "purported to exercise that authority." *Lindke v. Freed*, 601 U.S. 187, 198 (2024).

3. She did both. The Account carries her title [[and links to her official congressional website]]; her staff write and post to it; and it announces votes, committee action, and district events. *See* Compl. Ex. [[A]]–[[C]].

4. *Lindke* forecloses that defense where the official conducts government business on the account: "An official cannot insulate government business from scrutiny by conducting it on a personal page." 601 U.S. at 202 n.2.

5. If Defendant has since removed her title or the agency link, that is a fact to weigh, not a categorical defense. Here, by contrast, [[STATE WHAT REMAINS]].

## III. The Comment Space Is a Public Forum

6. Defendant says the Account is government speech. Her own posts may be. The replies are not: "while the President's tweets can accurately be described as government speech, the retweets, replies, and likes of other users . . . are not government speech under any formulation." *Knight First Amendment Institute v. Trump*, 928 F.3d 226, 239 (2d Cir. 2019).

7. Defendant opened the space. An account "intentionally opened for public discussion," used "as an official vehicle for governance," with interactive features "accessible to the public without limitation," is a public forum. *Id.* at 236.

8. Even if the Court classified the thread as a nonpublic forum, the result would be the same, because "\[v\]iewpoint discrimination is thus an egregious form of content discrimination," and the government "must abstain from regulating speech when the specific motivating ideology or the opinion or perspective of the speaker is the rationale for the restriction." *Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of the University of Virginia*, 515 U.S. 819, 829 (1995); *see Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, Inc.*, 473 U.S. 788, 806 (1985).

## IV. The Speech or Debate Clause Does Not Bar This Action

9. Defendant may invoke the Speech or Debate Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 6, cl. 1. The Clause protects legislative acts, not everything a Member does. The Supreme Court has confined it to "an act which was clearly a part of the legislative process," and has refused to extend it to "all things in any way related to the legislative process." *United States v. Brewster*, 408 U.S. 501, 515–16 (1972).

10. Most directly, the Court held that a Senator's newsletters and press release were not protected, because "neither the newsletters nor the press release was 'essential to the deliberations of the Senate' and neither was part of the deliberative process." *Hutchinson v. Proxmire*, 443 U.S. 111, 130 (1979).

11. The Tenth Circuit, surveying the cases, held that the Clause reaches "only 'legislative' acts by a member of Congress or an aide," and that "only official, formal acts (or perhaps their functional equivalent) deserve the adjective 'legislative.'" *Bastien v. Office of Senator Ben Nighthorse Campbell*, 390 F.3d 1301, 1305–06 (10th Cir. 2004). On that reasoning it held that a Senate office's "informal contacts with constituents and other sources of information and opinion were not legislative in nature." *Id.*

12. Administering a public comment channel and deciding who may use it is not voting, not committee work, and not the consideration of legislation. It is the operation of a communications channel. The Clause does not reach it.

## V. The Complaint States a Claim

13. Plaintiff has pleaded government action, the forum, her protected speech, the exclusion, and the viewpoint basis, with exhibits. [[IDENTIFY YOUR STRONGEST COMPARISON EXHIBIT.]] Because Plaintiff appears pro se, the complaint should be read to raise the strongest arguments it suggests.

14. The motion should be denied. In the alternative, Plaintiff requests leave to amend.
